lesson.title: Interrupting in casual conversations (with friends and family)
head: Purpose
Phrase
Example
rows: *Wait, wait. You quit your job? When?*

**Sorry, quick question…**
**Can I just say something?**
*Sorry, quick question. Who else was there?*
*Oh, that reminds me, did you ever get your phone fixed?*
*Before I forget, your mum called this morning.*
*Anyway, where was I? Oh yes, the hotel.*
*Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on, what did she say?*

lesson.title: Interrupting in professional settings (meetings, calls, presentations)
head: Purpose
Phrase
Example
rows: *Sorry to interrupt, but the client is waiting on line two.*

lesson.title: When someone interrupts YOU
head: Purpose
Phrase
Example
rows: *Good question, but if I could just finish my point first?*
**I'll come back to that in a minute.**
*That's a fair point. I'll come back to that in a moment.*
*As I was saying, the project should finish in June.*
*Oh, you wanted to say something? Please, go ahead.*
*Before we finish, does anyone have anything to add?*

lesson.label: 📖 Bài học chính
lesson.title: 1. Casual: Wait, he did what?!
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Linh, Tom and Mai are having coffee. Linh is telling them about a blind date last weekend. Her aunt organised it.*
lines: So, my aunt finally **set me up with** her colleague's son. We met at a small Italian restaurant on Saturday. He arrived twenty minutes late, and…
**Wait, wait.** Twenty minutes? Did he say sorry?
**Sort of.** He **blamed the traffic**, but he didn't seem very sorry. Anyway, we sat down and tried to **make small talk**.
**Sorry, quick question.** What does he do? Your aunt said he works at a bank, right?
Yeah. And that's the problem. He **spent** the first half hour **talking about** his money and his new car.
**Hang on a sec.** Half an hour? Did he ask you any questions?
**Not really!** When I tried to **change the subject**, he just gave me **one-word answers**. There were so many **awkward silences**. But wait, the worst part is coming.
**Oh, that reminds me**, my cousin **went on a date** like that last month. The guy **kept checking** his phone the whole time!
Ha, that's exactly what happened next! **Anyway, where was I?**
Oh, right. When the bill came, he said, "Shall we **split it**?" That's totally fine! But then he took out his phone and counted exactly what I ate, even one piece of garlic bread.
No way! That's **a red flag**. **Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on!**
**No worries.** Honestly, we had **nothing in common**, so I went home early. My aunt keeps asking if I'll **give him a second chance**. I don't think so!

lesson.title: 2. Professional: In the meeting
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Mr Harris, the team manager, is explaining a new plan for working from home at a team meeting. Laura and David are listening.*
lines: …so from next month, everyone will work from home on Mondays and Fridays, and come to the office from Tuesday to Thursday. We'll **try it for** three months, **as a trial**. It should **save** everyone **time** on **the commute**. During that time, I'd like…
**Sorry to interrupt, but could I just ask a quick question?**
Can we choose our home days, or are they **fixed**? I'd prefer something more **flexible**.
Good question. Each team can decide, but everyone needs to be **online and available** between ten and four.
**Can I just say something?** I'm **a bit worried about** team meetings. People **get distracted** easily on video calls, and it's much harder to **share ideas**.
**That's a fair point**, David. **I'll come back to that in a minute. Can I just finish first?**
Thanks. During the trial, I'd like everyone to **fill in** a short survey every two weeks. That way, we can **see how it's going**. Now, **going back to** David's point about meetings…
Yeah. It's just easier to share ideas **face to face**. On calls, it's **hard to know if** everyone understands, and some people never **turn their cameras on**.
**Can I just add something?** Maybe we could **keep** the big meetings **for** office days. Then home days could be for our own tasks, when we need to **stay focused**.
That's a great idea, Laura. It's **a good compromise**. **Is everyone happy with that?**
Great. **Before we move on, does anyone have any questions?**
Just one. Will the company give us any **equipment** for working from home, like a second screen? Some of us only have a small laptop.
I'm not sure yet. I'll **find out** and **get back to you** by Friday.

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Hannah has just started a new job. She meets her friend Sam for coffee.
lines: Pretty good! Yesterday, the team took me out for lunch so I could meet everyone.
At first, it was a bit strange. Nobody knew what to say, so we just tried to {make small talk} about the weather and the traffic. There were a few {awkward silences}.
Haha, that always happens at the start.
Then my manager started talking about work again, so I tried to {change the subject}. I asked everyone about their weekend plans, and that really helped.
Good idea. What's your manager like?
He's nice, but he seems quite {worried about} deadlines. He checked his emails all through lunch.
Not really. It's {hard to know} after just one lunch. I'll wait and {see how it goes}.
Fair enough. Do you work from home?
Two days a week. It saves me an hour on {the commute}, but at home, I {get distracted} really easily. My bed is right next to my desk!
So I prefer the office. It's much easier to work with people {face to face}.

I asked him about his holiday, but he only gave me {one-word answers}.
In my old job, the hours were {fixed}: 8am to 5pm, every day.
My new job is more {flexible}. I can start any time between eight and ten.

"Can we meet on Thursday at ten?" "Yes, {That works for me|that works for me}."
The company gave us new {equipment} for working from home: a laptop and a headset.
Sorry, the manager isn't {available} right now. She's in a meeting.
Please {turn your camera on} during video calls, so we can see you.

homework.title: Part 3A: Casual: a weekend trip
homework.instructions: Complete the conversation with phrases from the box. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Nam is telling his friends Lily and Hoa about his weekend trip to Đà Lạt.
bank: Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on!
lines: So, on the second day, we rented motorbikes and drove up into the mountains. Then it started raining really hard, and…
{Wait, wait.} You drove in the rain? Were you scared?
A bit! Anyway, we stopped at a small café to wait.
{Sorry, quick question.} Who did you go with? Your colleagues?
No, my cousins. So, we were sitting in the café, and…
{Oh, that reminds me}, did you try the strawberry milk? Everyone says it's amazing.
Yes, I had three glasses! {Anyway, where was I?} Oh yes, the café. The owner told us about a secret waterfall nearby.
A secret waterfall? Wow! {Sorry, I keep interrupting. Go on!}

homework.title: Part 3B: Professional: a team meeting
homework.instructions: Complete the conversation with phrases from the box. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Ms Chen is talking about the company's new website at a team meeting.
bank: I'll come back to that in a minute.
lines: …so the new website will be ready at the end of March. The design team will start next week, and…
{Sorry to interrupt, but} could I just ask a quick question?
Will customers be able to pay online?
{Can I just add something?} I think we should also have a live chat. Customers often have questions before they buy.
That's a fair point, Anna. {I'll come back to that in a minute.} {Can I just finish first?}
Thanks. {As I was saying,} the design team will start next week, and we'll test the website in early March.

homework.title: Part 4: Listening
homework.intro: Emma and Jack are colleagues. They're having lunch together after Emma's big presentation. Listen to the conversation, then choose the best answer.

script.text: So, how did it go? Was this your first time presenting to the CEO?
Yes, my first time. I was nervous, but I felt quite confident, because ==I practised it about ten times at home==. I knew every slide by heart.
Well, I started speaking, and everything was fine. But ==after about two minutes, my laptop suddenly went black==.
Wait, wait. Two minutes? That's so early!
I know! I tried to restart it, but it didn't work. In the end, ==someone from IT had to open my file on a different computer==. It took almost fifteen minutes.
Sorry, quick question. What did you do while you were waiting? Did the CEO take a break?
No, everyone just sat there, so I started talking without my slides. I told them a story about one of our customers and why she loves our product.
Oh, that reminds me, ==my manager always says people remember stories, not numbers==. Nobody remembers a chart, but everyone remembers a good story.

That's exactly what happened! When the slides came back, I showed the sales numbers at the end. But afterwards, ==the CEO said the customer story was her favourite part==. She said it was much more interesting than the numbers.
That's amazing! So, the laptop problem was actually a good thing.
Maybe! ==It went really well in the end==. But ==next time, I'm going to bring a copy of my slides on a USB stick==, just in case.
Good idea. And maybe start with a story too!

questions.q: Why did Emma feel confident at the start?
options: She had given a presentation to the CEO before.
A colleague had checked her slides.
questions.why: “I practised it about ten times at home.”

options: Near the end, during the sales numbers

Someone had to open the file on a different computer.

questions.q: Why does Jack talk about his manager?
options: To agree that people remember stories better than numbers
To warn Emma that the CEO doesn't like long presentations

options: She liked the sales numbers more than the story.
She found the unplanned part more interesting.
She thought the slides were too long.

questions.q: How does Emma feel about the laptop problem now?
options: It went well in the end, but she'll be more prepared next time.
